opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling matters a lot, but in math it looks a bit different from how people usually talk about it.

The standard story is that you scale data, compute, and parameters, and capabilities emerge. That has worked remarkably well for language, and it has carried models surprisingly far in math too. Models that a few years ago struggled with high school competition problems now do quite well on olympiad-level questions. So I don't want to dismiss scaling at all.

But mathematics has a property most domains don't: you can check whether an answer is actually right. If you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, the proof assistant either accepts it or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity and no human grader who might be fooled by something that sounds confident. That changes what scaling means. You're no longer only scaling pretraining on human-written text, which for math is fairly limited. Advanced mathematics is a small corpus compared to the whole internet. Instead you can scale verified experience. The model attempts proofs, the verifier tells it what works, and that becomes new training signal. In principle that loop can generate far more high-quality data than humans have ever written down.

So the way I see it, the next phase is scaling verification and search, not just model size. That means more compute at inference time, more exploration over proof strategies, and better formal libraries so the model has more mathematics to stand on. It's closer to the AlphaGo story than the pure next-token-prediction story. Self-play works when you have a reliable referee, and math gives you one.

There are real bottlenecks, though. One is autoformalization: most mathematics lives in papers written in natural language, and turning that into formal statements is still hard and error-prone. If you formalize the wrong statement, you can verify something perfectly and it means nothing. Another is that research math isn't just solving given problems. It's deciding which questions are interesting, which definitions are the right ones, and which conjectures are worth pursuing. I'm not sure scaling alone gets you mathematical taste, though I'm more optimistic than I used to be.

Long term, I think we'll see AI systems that work alongside mathematicians as genuine collaborators: proving lemmas, checking big arguments, exploring many directions in parallel. And because everything can be formally verified, mathematicians can trust the output without having to re-derive it line by line. That's the exciting part to me. Scaling plus verification could make mathematics both faster and more reliable at the same time, which almost never happens in science.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling has already carried models to strong olympiad-level performance and frames the next phase as scaling verification and search. It does not state that math AI has not yet been scaled like AI more broadly.

r002.rationale: It advocates scaling verification, search, inference compute, and formal libraries, but does not propose scaling math AI specifically to discover its performance ceiling.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes scaling and its bottlenecks, but does not suggest a cycle between scaling and renewed research.

fable-5.1.text:
Scaling has clearly worked for language, and I think it's working for mathematics too, but not in the way people first assumed. The naive version was: train a bigger model on more text, and eventually it learns to prove theorems. That gives you a model that sounds like a mathematician without being one. It writes a proof sketch that looks right, hand-waves the hard step, and never knows it did.

What changed the picture for me is pairing scale with verification. Once you have a formal system like Lean checking every step, the model gets a signal that can't be faked. Then scaling stops meaning "more internet text" and starts meaning "more search, more attempts, more verified trajectories." The compute goes into exploring the space of proofs rather than imitating the surface of proofs. That's a very different kind of scaling, and I think it's the one that matters for math.

At Axiom we think about it as scaling three things together. Model capacity, yes. But also the amount of inference-time compute you let the system spend on a single hard problem, because a real theorem might deserve hours or days of search, not a single forward pass. And the size of the formalized corpus itself, which is still small relative to what humans have written. Every proof the system verifies becomes training data that is guaranteed correct, so the system can bootstrap its own curriculum.

So I'm optimistic, but I'd put the emphasis differently from most. Mathematics is almost uniquely well-suited to scaling because the ground truth is checkable. The limiting factor isn't whether bigger models help. It's whether we can build the feedback loops that turn raw compute into verified knowledge. If we do, I think you get systems that don't just answer competition questions but actually push research mathematics forward, generating conjectures, closing lemmas, and letting human mathematicians work at the level of ideas rather than details.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes proof imitation from scaling with verification, but does not state that AI for mathematics has not yet been scaled in the way AI models more broadly have been.

r002.rationale: It advocates scaling model capacity, inference-time compute, and formalized corpora, but does not frame this as a way to discover AI’s performance ceiling.

r003.rationale: It describes feedback loops and verified knowledge bootstrapping, but does not suggest progress cycles between scaling and renewed research.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling will be important, but the question is what we’re scaling. There’s model size and training data, but there’s also the amount of computation a system can spend exploring a mathematical problem—trying an approach, checking it, and starting again when it fails.

Mathematics gives us an interesting opportunity because, when a problem is expressed formally, we can check a proposed proof precisely. That could support a feedback loop where systems generate arguments, verify them, and learn from successful attempts. But finding a proof and checking a proof are very different tasks. Having a reliable checker doesn’t automatically tell you which direction is promising.

So I’m interested in whether scaling produces better mathematical judgment: choosing useful definitions, identifying intermediate results, or recognizing that a different perspective makes a problem easier. I expect progress to come from combining scale with better ways to search and verify. The exciting outcome would be systems that help mathematicians explore ideas they couldn’t practically explore before.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible ways to scale mathematical AI but does not say it has not yet been scaled like AI models more broadly.

r002.rationale: It expresses interest in scaling and better search, but does not propose scaling specifically to discover a performance ceiling.

r003.rationale: It recommends combining scale with better search and verification, but does not describe progress cycling between scaling and renewed research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling will matter a great deal, but the question is what we scale. It’s not just model size or the amount of mathematical text in the training data. It’s also the amount of computation a model can use to explore an idea, test intermediate steps, and revise an argument.

Mathematics has a useful property here: when you work in a formal system, you can check whether a proof is valid. That gives you a feedback signal for training and search. But checking a proof and finding an interesting proof are very different tasks. A system could become extremely good at proving statements without being equally good at choosing which statements are worth pursuing.

So I’m excited about scaling as a way to expand what these systems can solve. The deeper question is whether that progress also produces better mathematical judgment: knowing when to introduce a new definition, try a different representation, or pursue a connection that initially looks unlikely. I’d want to measure progress on those dimensions too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what and how to scale, but does not state that AI for mathematics has not yet been scaled as broadly as AI models overall.

r002.rationale: It says scaling can expand what systems solve, but does not propose scaling to discover their performance ceiling.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe progress cycling between scaling and renewed research.
